title: Digital Wallet
problem: Design a digital wallet (PayPal/Venmo-style) that supports top-up from bank, ACID peer-to-peer transfers, and fast balance reads.
summary: A strongly consistent wallet built on a MySQL double-entry ledger, fronted by a Redis balance cache and a 2-phase-commit transfer coordinator that guarantees A→B money movements are atomic across two account shards. The dominant design choice is putting the canonical balance in ACID SQL (not in Redis) and using 2PC when sender and receiver live on different shards — accepting the ~30ms latency cost in exchange for zero reconciliation debt. Kafka is the audit spine: every state transition produces an immutable event that downstream fraud, analytics, and compliance systems consume independently.

functional: Top up a wallet from a linked bank account or card via an external rail (ACH, Stripe, UPI)
Transfer funds between two wallets atomically — either both sides move or neither does
Withdraw funds to a linked bank account with a hold period before the external rail settles
Serve a low-latency balance read (p99 < 20ms) for the app home screen
Maintain an immutable double-entry ledger of every money movement for audit
Enforce per-user KYC and per-transaction velocity limits before authorizing a transfer
nonFunctional: ACID guarantees on transfers — no lost updates, no phantom balances, no partial writes
Strong consistency on the write path; read-your-writes on the balance read path
p99 write latency under 200ms, p99 read latency under 20ms
Durability: zero ledger row loss; 7-year retention for regulatory audit
Availability 99.95% writes, 99.99% reads (balance read is served from replicas)
Horizontally scalable to 100M users without re-architecting the ledger

assumptions: Cache hit rate target: ≥ 99% on balance reads
SOX + PCI + regional banking regs → 7-year audit retention on every event
estimates: Ledger writes: 2 entries/transfer + 2 per top-up ≈ 30M rows/day, ~350 write TPS peak
Ledger storage: 30M * 365 * 7 * 250B ≈ 19 TB over 7 years — sharded MySQL by account_id
Redis balance cache: 500M accounts * ~80B ≈ 40 GB; a 3-shard cluster with 3 replicas each
Kafka audit log: 30M events/day * ~500B ≈ 15 GB/day, 38 TB over 7 years (cold tier after 30d)
Bank connector throughput bounded by partner bank (typical 50–200 TPS per partner, retries are expensive)

client.name: Client (Mobile / Web)
client.summary: PayPal/Venmo-style mobile app or web client.

sections.heading: Responsibilities
sections.body:
- Authenticate via OAuth2 + device binding
- POST /transfers with a client-side idempotency key (UUIDv4)
- GET /balance (frequent — every screen refresh in the app)

sections.heading: UX contract
sections.body: Users expect balance reads in <200ms end-to-end and transfer confirmation in <1.5s. Missing money is unacceptable even once — correctness beats latency every time.

sections.heading: Why this matters for beginners
sections.body: The client sees only two things that matter: their balance and whether a transfer went through. Every backend design choice serves those two guarantees.

bottlenecks.title: Balance polling storm on screen refresh
bottlenecks.trigger: Every screen refresh calls GET /balance; with 50M DAU and 200M balance reads/day (peak 10x ≈ 23K QPS), an app bug that polls on every render or a pull-to-refresh loop can 5-10x this overnight
bottlenecks.symptom: Redis cache CPU spikes, LB connection pool saturation, users see slower app scrolling as the device spends battery on HTTPS calls, and support tickets about battery drain
bottlenecks.mitigation: Client-side balance cache with 5-10s staleness window, coalesce concurrent in-flight /balance calls into one, subscribe to a push channel (WebSocket/APNs/FCM) for balance.changed events instead of polling, and enforce a per-device rate limit (e.g. 1 req/2s) at the API edge
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on p95 balance reads per device per minute > 30, and on ratio of /balance calls to /transfers exceeding 100:1 (baseline ~20:1 from 200M reads / 10M transfers)

bottlenecks.title: Idempotency-Key reuse or omission on retry
bottlenecks.trigger: Client code path retries POST /transfers after a network timeout without reusing the original UUIDv4 Idempotency-Key, or generates a new key on each tap; at 350 TPS peak even a 0.1% incidence = ~30K duplicate-risk transfers/day
bottlenecks.symptom: Double-charged users, duplicate ledger entries under different txn_ids, angry support tickets, and reconciliation alerts from the fraud/compliance consumer on wallet.transfer.committed
bottlenecks.mitigation: Generate the Idempotency-Key once at the moment the user taps Send and persist it in the client's local outbox DB until a terminal 2xx/4xx response is received; enforce SDK-level retry that always replays the same key; reject client builds missing the header at the API
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor txn_idempotency table for keys with >1 attempt and surface a 'duplicate_submit_rate' metric; alert if >0.05% of transfers in a 5-min window share from/to/amount within 60s but have different idempotency keys

bottlenecks.title: Stale JWT and step-up token handling
bottlenecks.trigger: JWTs expire (~42m in the flow) or the $500 step-up token expires (<5 min) mid-session; at 50M DAU with long app sessions, a meaningful fraction of transfer attempts hit an expired token right as the user taps Send
bottlenecks.symptom: User taps Send, sees a confusing 401/403, retries manually (possibly without idempotency-key preservation, compounding bottleneck #2), or abandons the transfer
bottlenecks.mitigation: Proactive token refresh at T-5min of expiry using refresh token; pre-flight a step-up challenge when amount_minor >= STEP_UP_THRESHOLD before showing the confirm button, not after; cache step_up_token and surface remaining validity in UI
bottlenecks.detection: Track client-side 'auth_expired_at_submit' event and server-side 401/403 rate on POST /v1/transfers; alert if >0.5% of transfer submits fail auth, or if median time between step-up completion and transfer submit exceeds 3 min

prebuild.explanation: ### Why the client is called out as a real component here For a digital wallet, the mobile/web client isn't just a dumb window onto the backend — it's actively responsible for two correctness-critical things that the server *cannot* do on its own. First, it generates the **idempotency key** (a UUID) the moment the user taps Send, and it reuses that same key on every network retry. Without that key originating on the device, the backend has no way to tell "user tapped Send twice because the network flaked" apart from "user genuinely wants to send $100 twice." Second, the client owns the UX contract: balance in under 200ms, transfer confirmation in under 1.5s, and *never* show a wrong number. Those constraints are what force the Redis cache, the pre-commit invalidation, and the 2PC design downstream. ### What happens without a well-behaved client Imagine the idempotency key is generated server-side instead. User taps Send, the request reaches the API, money moves on both shards, but the 201 response is lost to a dropped cellular connection. The app retries — new request, new server-side key, money moves *again*. Alice has now paid Bob $200 for a $100 lunch. Support tickets spike, the fraud consumer on `wallet.transfer.committed` starts flagging duplicates, and reconciliation engineers spend their weekend unwinding it. ### The numbers The design expects **200M balance reads/day vs 10M transfers/day** — a 20:1 read-to-write ratio. That's roughly 4 balance reads per active user per day (200M / 50M DAU), which only works if the client coalesces polling and honors a 5–10s local staleness window. A naive app that refetches on every render can easily 10x that to 2.3M QPS peak and melt the Redis cluster. ### The trade-off Trusting the client with the idempotency key means shipping SDK discipline to every platform — but the alternative (server-assigned keys) cannot survive lost responses, which is unacceptable for money.

lb.name: Load Balancer
lb.summary: L7 HTTPS load balancer across stateless wallet API replicas.

sections.heading: Algorithm
sections.body: Least-connections with health-check ejection after 3 consecutive 5xx within 10s.

sections.heading: TLS
sections.body: Public TLS terminated here; mTLS re-originated into the VPC. All downstream hops — ledger, cache, Kafka — require mTLS.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body: HA pair, multi-AZ anycast. Clients see at most one retry during a replica ejection; idempotency keys on mutating calls mean a retry is safe.

bottlenecks.title: TLS termination CPU exhaustion under polling storm
bottlenecks.trigger: 23K read QPS peak baseline on /balance, but a client polling bug can 5-10x that to 100K+ TLS handshakes/sec; with short-lived mobile connections (cellular churn), session resumption hit rates drop and every new connection costs a full ECDHE handshake (~2-5ms CPU per handshake)
bottlenecks.symptom: LB CPU pegged at 100%, handshake latency climbing from <5ms to 50ms+, 5xx spikes on /balance as the LB sheds load, on-call sees 'upstream healthy but clients timing out' — a confusing signature because API replicas look fine
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable TLS session resumption (session tickets with rotating keys, 24h lifetime) and TLS 1.3 0-RTT for idempotent GETs; offload ECDHE to hardware (AWS NLB+ACM or Nitro TLS, or dedicated TLS accelerator); enforce HTTP/2 on mobile clients so 23K QPS multiplexes over ~5K connections instead of 23K; pre-scale LB capacity to 3x observed peak
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on LB CPU > 70% sustained 2 min, TLS handshakes/sec > 2x transfer TPS baseline, and session_resumption_rate < 80%; dashboard the ratio of new_connections to requests

bottlenecks.title: Connection pool saturation during API replica ejection
bottlenecks.trigger: Health-check ejection after 3 consecutive 5xx in 10s can remove a replica carrying ~30% of connections (from the pool snapshot of ~28-35 conns/replica in the trace); at 23K read QPS peak with least-connections routing, surviving replicas absorb the redistributed load and their in-flight connection count can double in under 1s, exceeding per-replica concurrency=3000
bottlenecks.symptom: Cascading ejections — survivors also start returning 5xx as they saturate, the LB ejects them too, eventually all replicas marked unhealthy and fail-open mode returns 503 to clients; users see 'wallet unavailable' right when a single bad deploy was happening
bottlenecks.mitigation: Configure outlier detection with max_ejection_percent=33 so LB refuses to eject beyond 1/3 of the pool; add slow-start (gradual traffic ramp over 30s) when replicas rejoin to avoid thundering herd; set per-replica connection limits below the API's concurrency=3000 (e.g. 2000) so the LB queues rather than overwhelming; circuit-breaker with half-open probing
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on pool_healthy_ratio < 0.7, ejection_rate > 1/min, or p99 upstream_rq_time climbing > 200ms while backend CPU stays < 50% (signals queueing at the LB, not the app)

bottlenecks.title: Idempotent retry storm amplifying transfer load
bottlenecks.trigger: At 350 TPS peak transfers with failureRate=0.0001 at LB and 0.0005 at API, a brief API blip causes the LB retry filter to replay POST /v1/transfers; without careful config, retries can 2-3x the load on surviving replicas right when they're already struggling, pushing the 2PC coordinator past concurrency=500
bottlenecks.symptom: Transfer TPS doubles on dashboards during an incident, 2PC coordinator queue depth climbs, XA prepare timeouts cascade to ledger lock contention, users see 'transfer failed' even though the original eventually committed — now they've retried from the app too, compounding the storm
bottlenecks.mitigation: Configure retry budget (max 10% of request volume can be retries) and only retry on connect-failure/refused-stream, NEVER on 5xx for POST /v1/transfers; rely on client-side Idempotency-Key replay for app-level retries; set retry backoff with jitter (25-100ms); per-route timeout of 2s on transfer path so retries don't stack
bottlenecks.detection: Track lb_retry_ratio per route and alert if > 2% sustained; correlate with upstream_rq_retry_overflow counter (retries rejected by budget) — a rising overflow count means the budget is saving you from a storm

prebuild.explanation: ### Why the load balancer is here for a digital wallet The Wallet API is **stateless by design** — any replica can handle any request, because the truth lives in MySQL and Redis. That's a deliberate choice: it lets us run many API replicas in parallel to absorb the 23K peak read QPS on `/balance` plus 350 peak transfer TPS. But "many replicas" only works if something in front distributes traffic across them, ejects sick ones, and terminates TLS once so each replica isn't burning CPU on handshakes. That's the LB's job. It also enforces mTLS re-origination into the VPC — meaning every hop past this point (to the ledger, Redis, Kafka) is authenticated, which matters a lot when the payload is literally money movement. ### What happens without it Point DNS directly at one API replica and you've built a single point of failure for a payments system. One bad deploy, one OOM, one AZ blip → every user sees "wallet unavailable" mid-transfer. Worse, if a replica is half-dead (returning 5xx intermittently), clients retry `POST /v1/transfers` against the same broken box. The on-call sees a flood of timeouts, support tickets spike about stuck money, and the 2PC coordinator gets hammered with partially-completed protocol attempts it has to unwind. ### The number At **23K read QPS peak**, a single API replica handling ~2K QPS needs roughly 12 replicas just for reads. The LB's least-connections algorithm spreads that load evenly and ejects a replica after 3 consecutive 5xx in 10s — so one bad pod out of 12 costs you ~8% capacity for a few seconds, not 100%. ### The trade-off You've added an HA pair that itself must never fail — so the LB becomes critical infrastructure (multi-AZ anycast, pre-scaled TLS capacity) rather than something you can treat casually.

api.name: Wallet API
api.summary: Stateless REST/gRPC API for transfers, top-ups, and balance reads.

sections.heading: Endpoints
sections.body:
```
POST /v1/transfers (Idempotency-Key required)
POST /v1/top-ups (Idempotency-Key required)
GET /v1/accounts/:id/balance
```

sections.heading: Responsibilities
sections.body:
- Parse + validate request
- Call Auth to check token + device binding
- For reads: delegate to Balance Service
- For writes: delegate to 2PC Transfer Coordinator with a durable idempotency record

sections.heading: Request validation
sections.body:
- amount_minor must be a positive integer (minor units — cents); reject floats at the edge
- from_account must belong to the authenticated user
- currency must match both accounts; cross-currency transfers go through a separate FX path

lost: Harder to expose directly to web clients

bottlenecks.title: Concurrency cap exhaustion from blocking 2PC transfer calls
bottlenecks.trigger: API replica concurrency=3000, but POST /v1/transfers blocks waiting on the 2PC Transfer Coordinator (serviceTimeMs 10-50, p99 higher during XA prepare contention). At 350 TPS peak, if shard_11 locks queue and coordinator latency climbs from 30ms to 500ms, in-flight transfer requests can pin 175+ concurrency slots per replica; one slow shard turns the whole API pool into a queue
bottlenecks.symptom: All endpoints degrade simultaneously — even GET /balance slows because API worker threads are parked on transfer calls; LB starts ejecting replicas on 5xx despite backend DBs looking healthy; users see 'wallet unavailable' during what should be a localized shard hotspot
bottlenecks.mitigation: Isolate the transfer path with a bulkhead — dedicated thread/goroutine pool with cap (e.g., 800 of 3000 slots reserved for transfers, rest guaranteed for reads); hard 2s timeout on coordinator calls with 503 + Retry-After (client replays with same Idempotency-Key); deploy separate API replica pools for /transfers vs /balance if contention persists; circuit-breaker on coordinator with half-open probing
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on api_inflight_by_route where transfers > 50% of concurrency cap sustained 1min, p99 coordinator call latency > 200ms, and read-path p95 latency regression that correlates with transfer-path queue depth (cross-signal dashboard)

bottlenecks.title: Idempotency record insert contention on txn_idempotency table
bottlenecks.trigger: Every POST /v1/transfers and /v1/top-ups writes to txn_idempotency before delegating to the coordinator; at 350 transfer TPS + top-ups peak, plus client retry amplification on timeouts (same key replayed 2-3x per original), the table sees 1K+ INSERT-or-detect-duplicate ops/sec funneling through one shard (idempotency_key PK is not account-sharded in the schema shown)
bottlenecks.symptom: Transfer submission latency gains 20-100ms tail even when coordinator and ledger are healthy; hot-row contention on the idempotency table's PK index under retry storms; occasional deadlocks between idempotency insert and ledger_entries insert if they share a connection
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shard txn_idempotency by hash(idempotency_key) across the same 16 shards as the ledger, OR move it to Redis with SET NX EX (fall back to MySQL for the durable record, written async after the coordinator persists PREPARING); use INSERT... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE with a fast-path SELECT-first pattern; connection pool separation so idempotency writes don't starve ledger writes
bottlenecks.detection: Track p95 of the idempotency INSERT op separately, alert if > 10ms; monitor InnoDB row-lock-waits on the txn_idempotency table; alert if duplicate_key hits exceed 2% of submissions (signals retry storm + amplification)

bottlenecks.title: JWT verification CPU + Auth service fan-out on read path
bottlenecks.trigger: GET /v1/accounts/:id/balance at 23K peak QPS requires JWT signature verification on every call; even with 60s in-process positive cache, key rotation, cold replicas after deploy, or a JWT cache miss rate of 5% means 1,150 RSA/ECDSA verifies/sec per API pool. A deploy that rolls 12 replicas simultaneously empties all local caches at once
bottlenecks.symptom: Post-deploy latency spike on /balance from ~5ms to 30-50ms for 60-120s; API CPU spikes to 80%+ right after rolling deploys; Auth service QPS transiently 10-20x baseline as every replica re-verifies tokens it previously had cached
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use EdDSA (Ed25519) instead of RSA-2048 for JWTs — ~10x faster verify; warm the JWT verification cache pre-traffic via replay of recent tokens during replica readiness probe; stagger rolling deploys (max 2 replicas at once, 30s soak); move revocation check to a bloom filter refreshed every 10s instead of Redis round-trip; extend positive cache to match JWT TTL
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on api_cpu > 70% correlated with deploy events; track jwt_verify_cache_hit_ratio per replica with alert < 90%; monitor Auth service QPS and alert on > 3x baseline sustained 30s (signals cache stampede)

prebuild.explanation: ### Why the Wallet API is here For a PayPal/Venmo-style wallet, the API is the one place where every money-moving rule gets enforced *before* anything hits the ledger or the coordinator. It's the gatekeeper that says: "this amount is a positive integer in cents, not a float; this JWT actually belongs to the account being debited; this currency matches on both sides; this idempotency key either starts a new transfer or replays the result of a completed one." None of those checks belong in the 2PC coordinator (too late — locks are already being held) or in the client (can't be trusted with money rules). The API is also what lets us run many stateless replicas behind the LB to absorb the read fanout. ### What happens without it If clients talked straight to the coordinator, a malformed request — say, `amount: 10.005` as a float, or a JWT where `sub` doesn't match `from_account` — would reach XA PREPARE before being rejected, holding row locks on a MySQL shard for milliseconds of pointless work. A retry storm from a buggy app could hammer the ledger directly. Operators would see lock contention spikes and shard hotspots with no clear "blame" layer; users would see inconsistent error messages since each backend component has its own idea of a bad request. ### The number The design expects **23K peak read QPS on `/balance`** vs **350 peak transfer TPS** — a 65:1 ratio. A single API replica at concurrency 3000 handles roughly 2K QPS, so ~12 stateless replicas cover reads; they scale horizontally because the API holds zero session state. The ledger and coordinator, which *can't* scale as freely, are shielded by this layer doing cheap validation and JWT checks first. ### The trade-off Adding the API is an extra network hop (~5–15ms) on every call, accepted because correctness enforcement has to live somewhere the client can't bypass.

auth.name: Auth Service
auth.summary: Validates OAuth2 tokens + device binding + step-up challenges for high-value transfers.

sections.heading: Token validation
sections.body: Verify JWT signature, expiry, audience, and revocation (Redis blacklist). Cache positive results for 60s in-process.

sections.heading: Step-up auth
sections.body: Transfers above a configured threshold (e.g. $500) require recent (<5 min) biometric or SMS OTP confirmation. The Auth service issues a short-lived step_up_token the API must present.

sections.heading: Why separate
sections.body: Auth evolves fast (new MFA flows, device attestation); keeping it out of the wallet path lets it iterate without risking wallet correctness.

bottlenecks.title: JWT verification cache stampede on key rotation or mass restart
bottlenecks.trigger: With 23K peak read QPS on /balance + 350 TPS transfers all requiring JWT verify, the 60s in-process positive cache yields ~95%+ hit rates steady-state. But on signing-key rotation, a rolling deploy of the 12-replica API pool, or an Auth service restart, every token must be re-verified — potentially 20K+ RSA/ECDSA verifies/sec land on Auth at concurrency=3000
bottlenecks.symptom: Auth p99 climbs from 8ms to 200ms+, API replicas pile up waiting on verify calls, /balance latency regresses across the board, LB starts ejecting API replicas on 5xx even though the DB tier is healthy — on-call chases a ghost while Auth CPU is pegged
bottlenecks.mitigation: Switch JWT signing to Ed25519 (≈10x faster verify than RSA-2048); add a shared Redis L2 verification cache in front of Auth keyed by jti with 60s TTL so API replica restarts don't all hit Auth; stagger key rotation with a 10-min overlap window where both old and new kids are accepted; pre-warm JWT cache on API replica readiness probe via synthetic replay
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on auth_verify_qps > 3x baseline sustained 30s (signals cache miss storm), auth_cpu > 70%, or jwt_verify_cache_hit_ratio < 85% per replica; dashboard correlation between API deploy events and Auth QPS spike

bottlenecks.title: Revocation blacklist Redis round-trip on every verify
bottlenecks.trigger: Every token verification checks the Redis revocation blacklist (even on positive cache hit, the design implies revocation must be fresh). At 23K read QPS + 350 transfer TPS peak, that's ~23.4K Redis GETs/sec against the revocation store. A Redis failover (~5-15s unavailability) or a network partition to the revocation cluster blocks every auth decision
bottlenecks.symptom: All wallet operations stall simultaneously — reads AND writes — during a Redis blip; user sees 'wallet unavailable' on every screen; or if Auth is configured to fail-open on revocation-check errors, a revoked token (compromised device) can still transact for the duration of the outage, a compliance-grade incident
bottlenecks.mitigation: Replace Redis GET-per-verify with a bloom filter loaded into each Auth replica, refreshed every 10s from the revocation store — revocations propagate within 10s, verify cost drops to an in-memory bit check; keep Redis as the source of truth but make it off the hot path; explicit policy: fail-CLOSED on revocation-check unavailability for transfers, fail-open only for reads with a hard 30s budget
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on auth_revocation_redis_p99 > 5ms, revocation_fallback_rate > 0 (signals Redis unavailable), and revocation_bloom_staleness > 30s; dashboard ratio of verify_calls to revocation_store_calls — should be ~0 after bloom-filter rollout

bottlenecks.title: Step-up token validation hot path on high-value transfers
bottlenecks.trigger: Transfers ≥ $500 require a step_up_token issued by Auth and validated on every POST /v1/transfers. Assuming ~20-30% of the 350 TPS peak are above threshold (≈70-100 TPS), plus the SMS OTP / biometric issuance flow itself hits Auth. Step-up tokens are short-lived (<5 min) so cache reuse is minimal, forcing fresh cryptographic validation each time
bottlenecks.symptom: Tail latency on high-value transfers disproportionately worse than small ones (p99 of /transfers shows bimodal distribution around the $500 line); during a marketing event (e.g., rent-day, payroll), step-up issuance QPS spikes 5-10x and SMS provider rate-limits cascade into Auth timeouts, blocking legitimate large transfers
bottlenecks.mitigation: Sign step-up tokens with the same Ed25519 key so validation is a local signature check with no Auth round-trip — embed the step-up assertion as a claim in a short-lived JWT the API can verify itself; rate-limit SMS OTP issuance per-user (3/hour) and pre-warm biometric paths; fall back to in-app push approval (cheaper, faster) before SMS
bottlenecks.detection: Track p99 latency split by amount_minor >= STEP_UP_THRESHOLD and alert if the gap exceeds 50ms; alert on step_up_issuance_qps > 3x 7-day baseline; monitor SMS provider error rate and auth_step_up_fail_rate > 1%

prebuild.explanation: ### Why a separate Auth Service for a digital wallet For a PayPal/Venmo-style wallet, every single request — from a balance peek to a $10,000 transfer — has to answer two questions before anything else happens: *Is this token real, and is the person behind it allowed to move this much money right now?* Those checks are security-critical and change often (new MFA flows, device attestation, revoking stolen tokens fast), while the wallet's ledger logic is security-critical and must change *rarely*. Keeping Auth separate means the team can ship a new biometric challenge or rotate signing keys without touching code that moves money. ### What goes wrong without it Fold auth into the Wallet API and two bad things happen. First, a bug in a new MFA rollout — say, a token-validation regression — can accidentally reject valid transfers *or* accept revoked ones, and now your correctness bug is also a money bug. Second, high-value transfers need step-up auth (biometric/SMS OTP within 5 minutes); without a dedicated service issuing and validating the short-lived `step_up_token`, that logic gets smeared across every API replica, and a compromised device could drain an account before revocation propagates. Operators would see inconsistent auth behavior across replicas; users would see either false rejections or, worse, successful fraud. ### The number At **23K peak read QPS + 350 transfer TPS ≈ 23,350 auth checks/sec**, nearly every call needs token verification. The 60s in-process positive cache means ~95% hit rate, leaving ~1,170 fresh verifies/sec — a load big enough to need its own service, small enough that one tier of Auth replicas handles it. ### Trade-off An extra network hop (~2–8ms) on the hot path, accepted so auth logic can evolve independently of the ledger.

balance.name: Balance Service
balance.summary: Read path for account balances. Reads cache first, falls through to the ledger on miss.

sections.heading: Read algorithm
sections.body:
1. GET bal:{account_id}:{currency} from Redis
2. On hit (≥99% of reads), return immediately
3. On miss, SELECT balance_minor FROM account_balances on the ledger shard for that account and SETEX back
4. Emit a cache-miss metric — persistent >1% miss rate means Redis capacity is undersized

sections.heading: Consistency model
sections.body: Strongly consistent writes to the ledger invalidate the cache before committing. Readers either see the new balance (post-invalidate + fresh read) or the old balance briefly — never a torn/stale write-during-commit state. Formally: read-your-writes for the owner.

sections.heading: Why not compute from ledger entries per read
sections.body: 500M accounts, 23K read QPS peak — summing ledger_entries on every read would melt the DB. The materialized account_balances row is updated in the same transaction as the ledger entries, giving O(1) reads with zero correctness loss.

bottlenecks.title: Cache-miss stampede on hot accounts after invalidation
bottlenecks.trigger: Every transfer triggers `DEL bal:{from}:USD bal:{to}:USD` before commit. For a hot account (e.g., a merchant, creator, or popular Venmo user) receiving dozens of transfers/sec, the cache key is repeatedly invalidated while hundreds of concurrent /balance readers arrive. At 23K peak read QPS concentrated on even 0.01% of accounts, that's 2.3K QPS on a single key; after a DEL, all of them miss simultaneously and fall through to the same MySQL shard row.
bottlenecks.symptom: MySQL shard CPU spikes on one shard (the hot account's home), p99 balance reads climb from ~20ms to 200ms+, cache-miss rate jumps from <1% to 5-10% during viral moments, and the ledger shard's connection pool saturates even though overall system load looks normal
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use singleflight/request coalescing in the Balance Service — only one goroutine per (account_id, currency) fetches from MySQL on miss, others wait on the in-flight promise; add a short (1-2s) negative-lookup lock via `SET NX` in Redis so only one replica backfills; consider write-through (SET the new value instead of DEL) for the coordinator's invalidation path to eliminate the miss window entirely; add a small in-process LRU (100ms TTL) as L0 in front of Redis for ultra-hot keys
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on cache_miss_rate > 2% over 1min (baseline <1%), track singleflight_coalesced_requests per account and alert on top-K hot accounts exceeding 500 QPS, monitor ledger_shard_query_rate_from_balance_service and alert if it exceeds 5% of total read QPS

bottlenecks.title: Read-your-writes violation window between DEL and COMMIT
bottlenecks.trigger: The coordinator invalidates Redis BEFORE the XA COMMIT lands on both shards (~10-30ms window). A /balance read arriving during that window misses the cache, reads the ledger, and sees the PRE-commit balance (the committed row hasn't updated yet because XA is still in prepared state with the old committed value visible under READ COMMITTED). That stale value then gets SETEX'd back into Redis with a 300s TTL, poisoning the cache.
bottlenecks.symptom: User sends $100, sees success toast, pulls to refresh — balance still shows the old amount for up to 5 minutes until TTL expiry or the next write invalidates again; support tickets about 'money disappeared then reappeared'; intermittent, hard-to-reproduce because it requires the read to land in the 10-30ms coordinator window
bottlenecks.mitigation: Move invalidation to AFTER XA COMMIT completes on both shards (accept a brief window of stale-high reads, which is safer than stale-low for wallet UX); OR write-through the new balance from the coordinator post-commit instead of DEL; OR have the Balance Service check `version` column and refuse to cache a value if a concurrent coordinator_log entry for that account is in COMMITTING state; enforce READ COMMITTED + SELECT with a version fence
bottlenecks.detection: Synthetic canary that does transfer→read-immediately and asserts balance decreased; alert on balance_cache_version_regression counter (cache value has lower version than a subsequent ledger read); track p99 of time-between-commit and first-correct-read

bottlenecks.title: Per-request JWT ownership check fan-out on hot path
bottlenecks.trigger: Balance Service's upstream API does `jwt.claims.sub == owner_of("acct_alice")` on every /balance call. At 23K peak QPS, if `owner_of` is implemented as a lookup to a user→account mapping store (Redis or MySQL), that's another 23K QPS of metadata reads on the hot path. A cold mapping cache after deploy or a Redis blip on the ownership store stalls all reads — even though the balance cache itself is healthy.
bottlenecks.symptom: Balance read p95 doubles from ~15ms to 30-40ms after a rolling deploy; during an ownership-cache outage, /balance 5xx rate climbs despite Redis balance cache showing 99%+ hit rate; on-call confused because balance infrastructure dashboards look green
bottlenecks.mitigation: Embed the list of owned account_ids directly as a claim in the JWT at login time (bounded — most users own 1-3 accounts); verify ownership via a set-membership check on the decoded JWT with zero network calls; fall back to the ownership store only for users with >10 accounts (business accounts); cache owner_of lookups in-process with 5min TTL keyed by account_id
bottlenecks.detection: Track ownership_lookup_qps and alert if it approaches /balance QPS (should be ~0 after JWT-claim rollout); alert on owner_of_cache_miss_rate > 5%; dashboard correlation between post-deploy time and /balance p95 regression

prebuild.explanation: ### Why a dedicated Balance Service for this wallet In a PayPal/Venmo-style wallet, the balance is the single most-viewed piece of data in the entire system — every time a user opens the app, pulls to refresh, or lands on the home screen, they want to see their current balance *fast*. But balance is also derived from the ledger, which is the source of truth for money and must never lie. The Balance Service exists to reconcile those two pressures: it owns the read path, reads Redis first (where 99% of requests land), and falls through to the ledger only on a miss. Without this split, every balance peek would either hit MySQL directly (too slow, melts the DB) or trust Redis as truth (loses money on a pod restart). ### What happens without it Remove the Balance Service and the API either queries `account_balances` on every read — the ledger shards start seeing 23K QPS of point-lookups on top of the 350 TPS of 2PC writes, and lock contention between reads and XA-prepared transactions spikes tail latency — or worse, someone "optimizes" by summing `ledger_entries` on each read. With 19TB of ledger data and billions of rows, a single balance query now scans thousands of rows. Users see spinners; operators see MySQL CPU pegged; transfers start timing out because shards are busy serving reads. ### The number **200M balance reads/day vs 10M transfers/day — a 20:1 ratio.** At peak 23K read QPS with a ≥99% cache hit target, only ~230 QPS reach the ledger. Without the cache layer, MySQL would handle 23,000 QPS — roughly 100× more work — on top of write traffic. ### Trade-off A small staleness window during the invalidate-then-commit dance, in exchange for keeping the ledger focused on correctness rather than read throughput.

cache.name: Redis Balance Cache
cache.summary: Sharded Redis cluster holding hot account balances.

sections.heading: Key layout
sections.body:
```
bal:{account_id}:{currency} → balance_minor:int, updated_at:ts
TTL: 300s
```
Keys hash-slotted by account_id to keep reads and invalidations on the same shard.

sections.heading: Invalidation on write
sections.body: The Transfer Coordinator issues `DEL bal:{from_account}:USD bal:{to_account}:USD` BEFORE the MySQL COMMIT — a classic cache-aside with pre-commit invalidation. On rare Redis failure we fail-open on reads (allow stale within TTL) but NEVER fail-open on writes.

sections.heading: Why not cache as source of truth
sections.body: Redis is in-memory; a pod restart or shard failover can lose seconds of writes. For money, the source of truth must be durable + ACID — Redis accelerates reads, it doesn't own them.

lost: Invalidation fanout across API replicas is lossy; rare stale reads possible

bottlenecks.title: Hot-key contention on popular merchant/creator accounts
bottlenecks.trigger: With 23K peak read QPS spread across 500M accounts, a viral creator or high-volume merchant can concentrate 500-2000 QPS on a single `bal:{account_id}:USD` key. Since keys are hash-slotted by account_id to keep reads+invalidations on the same shard, one hot account pins all that traffic to ONE Redis shard (of 3), meaning that shard sees ~33%+ of total cluster QPS while siblings idle. Every transfer to/from that account also triggers a DEL, creating a miss-then-stampede cycle.
bottlenecks.symptom: One Redis shard at 80-100% CPU while others sit at 20%, p99 GET latency on that shard climbs from <1ms to 10-20ms, cache-miss rate spikes on invalidation causing 100s of concurrent ledger reads for the same row, MySQL shard hosting the hot account sees unexpected read QPS, on-call sees 'Redis is fine on average' dashboards while users of the hot account see laggy balance reads
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add a request-coalescing layer (singleflight) in Balance Service so only one goroutine per (account, currency) fetches on miss; use `SET NX` with a short (500ms) lock to serialize backfills; introduce an in-process L0 LRU cache (100ms TTL, bounded to 10K entries) on each Balance Service replica for ultra-hot keys — cuts Redis traffic for viral accounts by 10-100x; consider key-level replication (read replicas per hot shard) via Redis Cluster read-from-replica mode for identified hot accounts
bottlenecks.detection: Track per-key QPS via `redis-cli --hotkeys` sampling every 60s; alert on any single key >500 QPS or any shard_cpu >70% while cluster_avg_cpu <40%; dashboard top-20 hot keys and correlate with high-throughput accounts

bottlenecks.title: Invalidate-before-commit race producing stale cache poisoning
bottlenecks.trigger: The coordinator issues `DEL bal:{from}:USD bal:{to}:USD` BEFORE XA COMMIT lands on both shards (a 10-30ms window per the coordinator's 10-50ms serviceTime). At 350 TPS peak transfers × 2 invalidations each = 700 DEL/sec, and at 23K read QPS, the probability a /balance read lands in the gap between DEL and COMMIT is non-trivial — that read misses, falls through to MySQL, reads the PRE-commit balance (old value, since XA-prepared row isn't yet visible under READ COMMITTED), and SETEX's the stale value back with a 300s TTL.
bottlenecks.symptom: User sends money, sees success, pulls to refresh — balance shows the old value for up to 5 minutes (full TTL) unless another write invalidates again; support tickets about 'my money disappeared then came back'; race is intermittent and extremely hard to reproduce in staging because it requires sub-30ms timing
bottlenecks.mitigation: Switch to write-through post-commit: coordinator computes the new balance from the XA COMMIT ack and does `SET bal:...` with the fresh value AFTER both shards commit, eliminating the stale-read window entirely; alternatively, tag cache entries with a `version` and have Balance Service refuse to cache a value whose version is < the `coordinator_log` COMMITTING entry it saw; keep DEL as fallback for correctness; shorten TTL to 60s to bound worst-case staleness
bottlenecks.detection: Synthetic canary: perform transfer → immediate /balance read in a loop, assert new balance visible within 100ms; alert on any regression. Emit `cache_version_regression` counter when SETEX would overwrite a newer version; alert if >0 per minute

bottlenecks.title: Shard failover unavailability blocking 23K QPS of reads
bottlenecks.trigger: 3-shard Redis cluster with 3 replicas each means each shard owns ~1/3 of the 40GB keyspace and ~1/3 of the 23K peak read QPS (~7.7K QPS). A shard primary failover takes 5-15s (sentinel detect + promote + client rediscover). During that window, 7.7K QPS of reads fail or block, and the Balance Service's fail-open-on-read policy means they all cascade to the MySQL shard serving that account range — which normally sees 230 QPS from cache misses and suddenly gets 7.7K QPS.
bottlenecks.symptom: During a single Redis shard failover, 1/3 of /balance reads either error out or see 5-10s latency; MySQL shards hosting those accounts see connection-pool saturation and CPU spikes to 80%+; p99 on /balance climbs from ~30ms to 5000ms+; recovery extends beyond the Redis failover itself as MySQL catches up on backlogged queries
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable Redis client-side support for `READONLY` reads from replicas during primary failover (stale reads ok for ≤TTL window); configure client with fast failure detection (2s timeout, not default 30s) and exponential-backoff retry against replicas; deploy a circuit breaker in Balance Service that, on sustained shard unavailability, rate-limits MySQL fallback to 2x normal miss rate (~460 QPS) rather than unleashing 7.7K QPS stampede; run quarterly game-day failover drills to validate recovery SLA
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on redis_shard_availability <100% for >2s, ledger_read_qps_from_cache_miss >3x baseline (signals stampede in progress), and Balance Service fallback_to_ledger_rate >5%; track client-observed Redis p99 latency per shard separately so one bad shard is visible amid two healthy ones

prebuild.explanation: ### Why Redis sits in front of the ledger here For a PayPal/Venmo-style wallet, the balance is the single most-requested number in the whole system — users open the app and the first thing they want to see is "how much do I have?" The ledger (MySQL) is where the *truth* lives, because money demands ACID guarantees and double-entry bookkeeping. But MySQL is also busy holding row locks during 2PC transfers, and it's sharded across 16 nodes. Pointing every balance read at it would put read traffic in direct contention with the write path that actually moves money. Redis exists to absorb that read load so the ledger can focus on correctness. ### What goes wrong without it Remove the cache and every app screen-refresh becomes a query against a sharded MySQL cluster that's simultaneously running XA-prepared transactions. Users see the app feel sluggish; the on-call sees MySQL CPU climb, lock waits grow, and p99 transfer latency spike because balance `SELECT`s are queueing behind the coordinator's `UPDATE`s. A single viral moment — a popular creator getting tipped — could cascade from "hot account" into "shard hotspot" into "transfers timing out." ### The number Capacity says **200M balance reads/day vs 10M transfers/day — a 20:1 read/write ratio**, peaking at **23K read QPS**. With a 99% cache hit rate, only ~230 QPS reach MySQL. Without Redis, that's 23,000 QPS of point-lookups hammering the same shards already handling ~350 transfer TPS worth of locking. ### The trade-off You accept a brief invalidation window (and the complexity of keeping cache and ledger in sync via pre-commit `DEL`) in exchange for sub-millisecond reads and a ledger that isn't melting.

coord.name: 2PC Transfer Coordinator
coord.summary: Coordinates the A→B transfer across (possibly) two MySQL shards using two-phase commit + a durable coordinator log.

sections.heading: Why 2PC here
sections.body: Account A and account B may live on different MySQL shards (sharded by account_id). A single local transaction can't cover both. 2PC gives us atomicity: either both shards commit the debit/credit or neither does.

sections.heading: Protocol
sections.body:
```
1. txn_id = new_txn; persist { status=PREPARING, from, to, amount } in coordinator log
2. PREPARE phase — send to both shards: shard_from: BEGIN; UPDATE balances SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE account=A AND balance>=100; XA PREPARE 'txn_id' shard_to: BEGIN; UPDATE balances SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE account=B; XA PREPARE 'txn_id'
3. If either PREPARE fails → XA ROLLBACK on both; mark ABORTED; return error
4. If both vote YES → persist COMMITTING; send XA COMMIT 'txn_id' to both shards
5. Persist COMMITTED; publish TransferCompleted to Kafka
```

sections.heading: Crash recovery
sections.body: If the coordinator crashes mid-protocol, the log tells us what to finish. PREPARING with neither side prepared → safe to abort. COMMITTING → must drive COMMIT on both sides on restart (cannot abort; already promised).

sections.heading: Why not Saga/eventual consistency
sections.body: A Saga leaves a window where one side debited without the other credited, visible to users and to fraud. Product constraint at PayPal/Venmo is: never display a balance that doesn't sum across the system. 2PC pays ~30ms for that guarantee; we spend it.

sections.heading: Same-shard fast path
sections.body: If A and B are on the same MySQL shard (hash(account) matches), we skip 2PC entirely and run a single local transaction — ~5–10ms instead of ~30ms.

gained: No blocking locks across shards; higher throughput
lost: Compensations are another source of bugs for money movement

bottlenecks.title: Coordinator log write becomes the global serialization point for all cross-shard transfers
bottlenecks.trigger: Every cross-shard transfer requires 3 durable writes to coordinator_log (PREPARING → COMMITTING → COMMITTED) before the user gets a 201. At 350 TPS peak with ~70% cross-shard (assume even hash distribution across 16 shards → ~94% cross-shard), that's ~330 TPS × 3 = ~1K durable log writes/sec funneling through whatever backs the log. If the log is a single MySQL row-per-txn table with fsync-per-write, commit latency floor is ~5-10ms × 3 = 15-30ms of pure log overhead on every transfer, and the log itself becomes a throughput ceiling well before the ledger shards do.
bottlenecks.symptom: Transfer p99 latency floors at 50-80ms even when both ledger shards are idle; coordinator concurrency=500 fills during any log-storage blip; on-call sees healthy MySQL shards, healthy Redis, healthy Kafka, but transfer latency inexplicably elevated — the log tier is the hidden bottleneck and doesn't appear on most dashboards
bottlenecks.mitigation: Back coordinator_log with a dedicated replicated log (Raft-based like etcd/FoundationDB, or a dedicated MySQL cluster with group commit + binlog_group_commit_sync_delay=1ms to batch fsyncs); collapse PREPARING+COMMITTING into a single write where protocol allows (the COMMITTING entry alone is the point-of-no-return anchor); partition the coordinator log by txn_id hash so multiple log shards absorb the 1K writes/sec; pre-allocate txn_ids in batches to avoid round-trips
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on coordinator_log_write_p99 > 10ms, coordinator_log_writes_per_sec approaching capacity of the underlying store, and ratio of (transfer_p99 - max(shard_prepare_p99, shard_commit_p99)) > 20ms sustained 2min (signals log overhead dominates); dashboard per-phase latency breakdown (PREPARING-write, PREPARE-RPC, COMMITTING-write, COMMIT-RPC, COMMITTED-write)

bottlenecks.title: Stuck COMMITTING state after partial XA COMMIT ack requires forward-recovery, blocking shard rows
bottlenecks.trigger: After coordinator writes COMMITTING, it must drive XA COMMIT on both shard_3 and shard_11. If one shard acks and the other times out (network blip, shard failover, 5-15s unavailability), the coordinator cannot abort — it has already promised. At 350 TPS with coordinator failureRate=0.001 and p99 XA COMMIT latencies of tens of ms, even a single-shard 10s blip strands ~50-100 transactions in COMMITTING with one side committed and the other still in XA-prepared state holding row locks.
bottlenecks.symptom: Specific accounts show 'ghost' behavior — debit landed, credit didn't (or vice versa) visible to balance reads; rows on the lagging shard locked for seconds-to-minutes pending XA COMMIT retry, causing any subsequent transfer touching those accounts to queue on lock wait; Kafka wallet.transfer.committed event is delayed or missing for these txns, confusing downstream fraud/analytics; user sees inconsistent balances between sender and recipient
bottlenecks.mitigation: Coordinator MUST have a forward-recovery worker that scans COMMITTING entries every 1s and retries XA COMMIT on the unacked shard with exponential backoff + unbounded retry (this is correct — we promised); persist per-shard ack state in the log entry so retries only target the lagging shard; set XA COMMIT timeout to 2s with immediate retry rather than failing; emit wallet.transfer.committed to Kafka only after BOTH shards ack to avoid downstream confusion; run a janitor that alerts (not aborts) on any COMMITTING entry older than 30s
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on any coordinator_log entry in COMMITTING state older than 10s, xa_commit_retry_count per txn > 3, per-shard partial_commit_count > 0/min; synthetic canary that kills one shard's connection mid-COMMIT weekly and verifies recovery drives both sides to COMMITTED within 5s; dashboard gap between COMMITTING-write-ts and COMMITTED-write-ts with p99 < 100ms SLO

bottlenecks.title: Concurrency=500 cap exhausted by lock-hold time on hot-account contention
bottlenecks.trigger: Coordinator concurrency=500 with serviceTimeMs 10-50 supports ~10K-50K TPS theoretically, but real throughput is bounded by lock-hold time on contended rows. A viral merchant receiving 50 TPS has 50 concurrent coordinator slots holding XA-prepared locks for the full PREPARE→COMMIT window (20-60ms); cross-shard round-trip variance and coordinator_log fsync latency extend this to 100-200ms under load. At 350 TPS peak with even mild hot-account skew, 200+ of the 500 slots can pin on a single hot row, leaving <300 slots for the rest of the system.
bottlenecks.symptom: Transfer submissions to non-hot accounts also slow down or get rejected with 503; coordinator in_flight climbs to cap while ledger shards show only moderate CPU; the bulkhead at the API layer (800 slots reserved for transfers) drains faster than expected; LB sees POST /v1/transfers 503 rate climb even though individual ledger shards look healthy
bottlenecks.mitigation: Bulkhead the coordinator pool by target-account-shard (e.g., 50 slots per shard of 16 = 800 total, preventing one hot shard from starving others); add hot-account detection that routes credits for identified merchants to sub-bucket accounts (credit-bucketing pattern) aggregated by a reconciler, eliminating single-row contention; short-circuit same-shard transfers onto a separate concurrency pool (they don't need the 2PC machinery); increase concurrency to 2000 with per-shard caps once bulkheaded
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on coord_in_flight > 400 sustained 60s, per-target-account concurrent-holds > 20, and p99 coordinator service time > 150ms while ledger p99 < 40ms (signals queueing at coordinator, not DB); dashboard top-20 hot accounts by concurrent coordinator slot occupancy

prebuild.explanation: ### Why the coordinator exists for this wallet In a PayPal/Venmo-style wallet, Alice's account and Bob's account might live on *different* MySQL shards — because with 500M accounts, no single database box holds everyone. A normal SQL transaction (`BEGIN... COMMIT`) only works within one database. So when Alice sends Bob $100, we need something that can reach into two separate databases and make sure **either both of them change, or neither does**. That's the coordinator's entire job: run two-phase commit (2PC) across the two shards so the system never ends up in a state where Alice was debited but Bob wasn't credited (or vice versa). ### What goes wrong without it Imagine we just did two independent UPDATEs: debit Alice on shard 3, then credit Bob on shard 11. The second call fails — network blip, shard failover, OOM. Alice's $100 is gone; Bob never got it. The user sees "transfer succeeded" then a wrong balance; support gets a panicked ticket; the reconciliation team spends the weekend reading ledger entries to figure out which of last night's 10M transfers half-landed. The ledger invariant (sum of all balances is constant) is broken, and there's no automated way to fix it. ### The number At **10M P2P transfers/day with a 16-shard ledger**, the odds that a random transfer stays on one shard are ~1/16 ≈ 6%. So **~94% of transfers cross shards** — roughly 9.4M per day need 2PC. The coordinator isn't an edge case; it's the main path. ### The trade-off 2PC adds ~30ms of latency per cross-shard transfer (extra PREPARE round-trip + durable log writes), accepted in exchange for zero reconciliation debt on money movement.

ledger.name: Ledger (MySQL, Double-Entry, Sharded)
ledger.summary: Authoritative double-entry ledger. MySQL InnoDB sharded by account_id. XA transactions used by the coordinator.

sections.heading: Schema
Sharding
sections.body: Shard key = account_id hash, 16 shards. A transfer whose accounts land on different shards triggers 2PC; same-shard transfers are a single local BEGIN/COMMIT. Rebalancing is done via dual-write + verify + cutover (never a live data move).

sections.heading: Balance invariant (never negative)
sections.body: `UPDATE account_balances SET balance_minor = balance_minor -:amt WHERE account_id =:a AND currency =:c AND balance_minor >=:amt` — the `balance_minor >=:amt` predicate is the overdraft guard. If 0 rows are updated, the transfer is rejected as insufficient balance.

sections.heading: Money type
sections.body: BIGINT minor units (cents). No DECIMAL arithmetic in the hot path; formatting to dollars happens only at the edge. Float balances are the single most common bug that ships to production and the single most expensive to unwind.

sections.heading: Why MySQL + XA
sections.body: Mature XA support in InnoDB, well-understood ops. Postgres works equally well; CockroachDB/Spanner would let us skip 2PC at the cost of tail latency and operational complexity.

gained: Stronger constraint system (partial indexes, CHECK constraints)
lost: Smaller talent pool in some orgs

gained: Global strong consistency — no app-level 2PC needed

bottlenecks.title: XA prepared-transaction lock hold time on cross-shard transfers
bottlenecks.trigger: At 350 peak transfer TPS with the coordinator's 10-50ms serviceTime, XA PREPARE holds row locks on `account_balances` for acct_alice/acct_bob until XA COMMIT lands — a 20-60ms window per transfer. Hot accounts (popular merchants, creators receiving many tips) concentrate many PREPAREs on the same row, so lock waits queue; a coordinator stall or network blip between PREPARE and COMMIT extends hold times into seconds, and with ledger concurrency=300 per shard, even 10-20 queued waiters on one hot row can stall an entire shard's transfer throughput
bottlenecks.symptom: Transfer p99 latency climbs from ~50ms to 500ms+ for any transaction touching the hot account; InnoDB `Innodb_row_lock_waits` spikes on one shard while others look idle; 2PC coordinator sees XA PREPARE timeouts cascading into ABORTs; users of non-hot accounts also suffer because the coordinator's concurrency=500 pool fills with stuck transactions
bottlenecks.mitigation: Set `innodb_lock_wait_timeout=3` (not default 50s) so stuck PREPAREs fail fast and free the coordinator; enforce a 2s deadline on the PREPARE→COMMIT gap in the coordinator with auto-rollback; for known hot accounts (merchants), use an account-sharded sub-ledger pattern where credits write to N shadow rows (credit bucketing) and a background reconciler sums them, eliminating single-row contention; monitor and pre-split hot accounts
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `innodb_row_lock_time_avg > 20ms` per shard, `Innodb_row_lock_waits/sec > 50`, and XA-prepared-transactions-in-flight > 100 sustained 30s; dashboard top-10 contended rows via `performance_schema.data_lock_waits` and alert on any row with >20 waiters

bottlenecks.title: Orphaned XA-prepared transactions from coordinator crash blocking shard
bottlenecks.trigger: If the coordinator crashes between XA PREPARE and XA COMMIT (the COMMITTING state in its log), the prepared transaction on each shard holds its row locks indefinitely — InnoDB will NOT release them on connection close because XA prepared state is durable. At 350 peak TPS with a coordinator failureRate=0.001, ~0.35 crashes/sec worth of in-flight transactions × 20-60ms hold window = dozens of orphaned prepared txns possible during a bad coordinator deploy; each one pins a row and consumes an undo-log slot
bottlenecks.symptom: After a coordinator incident, specific accounts become 'frozen' — every subsequent transfer touching them hangs on lock wait and times out; `XA RECOVER` on the shard shows dozens of prepared-but-not-committed txns; on-call sees healthy DB metrics but user-reported 'transfers stuck' for specific accounts; undo-log grows and ibdata1 bloats if recovery is delayed hours
bottlenecks.mitigation: Coordinator MUST run a recovery scan on startup that reads its durable log and drives XA COMMIT or XA ROLLBACK for every non-terminal entry before accepting new traffic; run a janitor job every 60s that calls `XA RECOVER` on each shard and cross-references with coordinator_log — any prepared txn older than 30s with no coordinator entry gets `XA ROLLBACK`ed; set `innodb_max_undo_log_size` alerts; never use coordinator state that can be wiped on redeploy (persist to replicated storage, not local disk)
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `XA RECOVER` count > 5 per shard, any prepared txn age > 60s, coordinator_log entries in PREPARING/COMMITTING state older than 10s; synthetic canary: kill coordinator mid-transfer in staging weekly and verify recovery clears prepared state within 5s

bottlenecks.title: Cross-shard rebalancing and shard hotspotting as accounts grow asymmetrically
bottlenecks.trigger: Schema shards by hash(account_id) across 16 shards, expecting even distribution of 500M accounts. But transfer volume is highly skewed — a handful of merchant/platform accounts (e.g., a Venmo business account, a creator-payout hub) may see 10-100x the TPS of consumer accounts. Over time one shard can absorb 20%+ of the 350 TPS transfer load (70+ TPS on a single shard with concurrency=300) while siblings idle at 20 TPS; the 19TB / 16 shards = ~1.2TB per shard assumes balanced growth that won't hold
bottlenecks.symptom: One shard shows 80% CPU and IO utilization while others sit at 15%; p99 transfer latency is bimodal — fast for non-hot-shard transfers, slow for anything touching the hot shard; storage on hot shard fills faster than forecast, forcing emergency resharding; the 'rebalancing via dual-write + verify + cutover' process takes weeks per shard split and blocks other work
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add a second-level shard key for high-throughput account types — e.g., hash(account_id + sub_bucket) with 4-16 sub-buckets per merchant account, aggregated by a background reconciler; proactively pre-split merchant/platform accounts onto dedicated shards (shard-per-tenant pattern) before they become hot; automate the dual-write + verify cutover pipeline so rebalancing takes hours not weeks; monitor shard imbalance continuously and trigger splits at 2x-of-median load
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on per-shard TPS > 2x cluster median sustained 10min, per-shard storage > 1.5TB (90% of 1.2TB target), per-shard CPU > 70% while cluster average < 40%; weekly report of top-100 accounts by TPS with warning when any account crosses 10 TPS sustained

prebuild.explanation: ### Why the ledger is the heart of this wallet For a PayPal/Venmo-style wallet, the ledger is the one place in the system where money *actually exists*. Every other component — the Redis cache, the Kafka event log, the API — is either an accelerator or an audit trail. The ledger is the source of truth, and it's MySQL specifically because money movement demands ACID guarantees: either Alice's debit and Bob's credit both commit, or neither does. It uses **double-entry bookkeeping** (every transfer writes two rows in `ledger_entries`, one debit and one credit) so the sum across all accounts is always zero — a self-checking invariant that catches bugs before they become lost money. And it's **sharded by account_id** because no single MySQL box can hold 500M accounts' worth of balances and history. ### What goes wrong without it Imagine storing balances only in Redis. A pod restart or AZ failover loses the last few seconds of writes — which in a wallet means real users lose real dollars. The on-call sees reconciliation alerts fire, support gets flooded with "my money disappeared," and there's no authoritative record to replay from. Kafka has the events, but without a durable transactional store, you can't atomically update a balance *and* publish an event — you'd get phantom transfers or silent drops. ### The number Capacity says **~30M ledger rows/day × 365 × 7 years × 250B ≈ 19 TB**. Divided across 16 shards, that's ~1.2 TB per shard — a size MySQL/InnoDB handles comfortably, whereas a single unsharded box would choke on both storage and the ~350 write TPS peak. ### The trade-off Choosing MySQL + XA means paying ~30ms per cross-shard transfer for 2PC, accepted in exchange for zero reconciliation debt.

bank.name: Bank Connector
bank.summary: Outbound gateway to partner banks (ACH, SEPA, FedNow). Rate-limited per partner and retried carefully.

sections.heading: Protocol
sections.body: Typical real-world: REST over HTTPS with OAuth2 client-credentials for modern partners (Plaid, Stripe Financial Connections, local instant-payment rails), or SFTP NACHA files for legacy ACH.

sections.heading: Latency / failure profile
sections.body: External call to another institution — p50 400ms, p95 1s, p99 several seconds. Failure rate 0.5% baseline, 5%+ during bank maintenance windows. An order of magnitude worse than any internal component.

sections.heading: Idempotency + retries
sections.body: Every bank request carries a wallet-generated `client_ref_id`. On timeout, we retry with the same ref — the bank dedupes. But retries are NOT free: each one may cost a partner transaction fee, so we cap retries at 3 with exponential backoff and surface the rest to the reconciliation pipeline.

sections.heading: Status model
sections.body: Top-ups from banks are NOT instantly credited. Flow: `submitted → bank ack → settled (T+1 or T+0 with FedNow)`. The wallet shows `pending` balance until settlement; `available` balance updates on settled.

bottlenecks.title: Partner bank rate-limit saturation during peak top-up bursts
bottlenecks.trigger: Bank Connector concurrency=200 against a partner ceiling of 50–200 TPS per bank. A payday spike or marketing event can push top-up submissions from baseline ~100 TPS to 500+ TPS against a single partner (e.g., Chase); with p95 bank latency of 1s, even 200 in-flight requests saturate the pool, and the partner starts returning 429s or silently queueing
bottlenecks.symptom: Top-up submissions pile up in the coordinator with status=PENDING_BANK for minutes, user sees Add Money spinner then 'try again later', 429/503 rate from partner climbs, and a thundering-herd of retries (each carrying per-transaction fees) hits right after the partner recovers
bottlenecks.mitigation: Per-partner token-bucket rate limiter sized to 80% of the partner's published TPS (e.g., 160 TPS for a 200 TPS partner), backed by a Redis-backed distributed limiter so all Bank Connector replicas share the budget; queue excess submissions in a durable work queue (SQS/Kafka) with FIFO per-partner ordering and surface 'estimated_settle_at' += queue_delay to the client; circuit-breaker per partner that opens on 429 rate > 2% and half-open probes every 30s
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on per-partner in_flight_requests > 80% of concurrency cap sustained 60s, partner_429_rate > 1%, and queue_depth_by_partner > 5min of drain time; dashboard per-partner p99 latency and rate-limit headroom

bottlenecks.title: Settlement webhook loss or delay leaving top-ups stuck in pending
bottlenecks.trigger: Top-ups sit in PENDING_BANK until the partner posts a settlement webhook (T+0 FedNow to T+1 ACH). A missed webhook (partner outage, our endpoint 5xx during a deploy, signature mismatch after key rotation) or a multi-hour partner settlement delay leaves user funds invisibly frozen. At 10M transfers/day implied scale, even 0.1% webhook loss = thousands of stuck top-ups/day, each one a support ticket
bottlenecks.symptom: Users complain 'I added $500 yesterday, it's still pending', pending_minor grows unboundedly on specific accounts, the reconciliation team gets paged with mismatches between bank statement totals and wallet top_ups.status='settled' counts, and available_minor never catches up
bottlenecks.mitigation: Never rely solely on webhooks — run a reconciler that polls the partner's GET /transactions?since=T API every 5 min for all top-ups in PENDING_BANK older than expected_settle_at, and drives the settled state transition idempotently; webhook endpoint must be idempotent (dedupe on bank_txn_id) and persist raw payload before ACK; alert on any top-up stuck in pending > 2x expected_settle_at; daily bank-statement reconciliation job that diffs partner EOD file against top_ups table
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on count(top_ups WHERE status='pending' AND created_at < now - INTERVAL '36 hours') > 0 for ACH or > 10 min for FedNow; track webhook_received_count vs bank_txn_created_count ratio per partner and alert if < 99% over 1h window; monitor reconciler_mismatches_per_day > 50

bottlenecks.title: Retry amplification on ambiguous bank timeouts causing duplicate debits
bottlenecks.trigger: Bank Connector p99 latency is several seconds with failureRate=0.005 (5% during bank maintenance). On a read timeout, the coordinator can't tell if the partner accepted the debit or not — retrying (up to 3× per design) with the same client_ref_id depends on the partner honoring idempotency, which some legacy ACH rails do NOT. A 10-min bank blip at 100 TPS = 60K ambiguous transactions, each potentially retried 3×
bottlenecks.symptom: After a bank incident, reconciliation finds duplicate BNK-* txn_ids charged against the same client_ref_id, or the opposite — client_ref_ids with no corresponding bank txn that actually settled anyway; customer-facing double-debits that require manual refund via bank ops; per-transaction fees billed 2–3x
bottlenecks.mitigation: Never retry a POST to the bank on read-timeout without first calling GET /transactions?client_ref_id=X to check current state; implement per-partner retry policy matrix (idempotent partners: safe retry; non-idempotent: status-check-first); cap retries at 3 with exponential backoff + jitter (500ms, 2s, 8s) and route exhausted retries to a human-reconciliation queue, not auto-abort; keep client_ref_id stable across all retries of the same txn_id
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on bank_retry_rate > 5% (baseline < 1%), count of (client_ref_id, bank_txn_id) pairs where 1 client_ref maps to >1 bank_txn > 0/day, and partner_fee_per_successful_topup trending up week-over-week (signals silent retry waste)

prebuild.explanation: ### Why the Bank Connector exists for this wallet A digital wallet is useless if money can't get *into* it. Users top up from their bank (Chase, BofA, etc.) via ACH, SEPA, or FedNow — and every single one of those rails is a different external system, each with its own auth, latency, retry rules, and failure modes. The Bank Connector is the one place that speaks "bank protocol" so the rest of the wallet doesn't have to. It also isolates the *scariest* part of the system: calls that leave our datacenter, cost real money per attempt, and can silently double-charge a user if retried wrong. ### What happens without it Imagine the Wallet API calling Chase's ACH endpoint directly. A network blip mid-request, the API retries naively, and Alice gets debited twice for the same $500 top-up. The operator sees reconciliation mismatches the next morning; support fields angry tickets; and the ledger now has a phantom `pending` row that never settles. Worse, a bank maintenance window (5%+ failure rate) cascades into the 2PC coordinator, which starts holding row locks waiting on a 10-second external call — and suddenly peer-to-peer transfers between internal accounts slow down too, because the coordinator's concurrency pool is full of stuck bank calls. ### The number Partner banks cap throughput at **50–200 TPS per partner**, while our internal peak is **350 transfer TPS**. That's a 2–7× mismatch — the connector *must* rate-limit, queue, and backpressure, or we'll get 429s that cascade into user-visible failures. ### The trade-off We accept an extra hop (~400ms p50) and an async `pending → settled` UX in exchange for never letting external-bank flakiness corrupt our internal ledger.

kafka.name: Kafka Event Log
kafka.summary: Append-only audit spine. Every state transition publishes an immutable event.

sections.heading: Topics
sections.body:
```
wallet.transfer.prepared (intent; PII-scrubbed)
wallet.transfer.committed (final; consumed by fraud, analytics, compliance)
wallet.topup.settled (bank rails)
wallet.balance.changed (delta stream for downstream caches)
```

sections.heading: Delivery model
sections.body: Producer with `acks=all`, min.insync.replicas=2, RF=3. Transactional producer semantics for exactly-once coupling with the MySQL commit (Debezium-style outbox or KIP-939 XA extensions).

sections.heading: Retention
sections.body: 7 days hot on Kafka itself; tiered storage to S3 after that for 7-year audit retention. Downstream consumers (fraud, analytics, regulatory reports) read from the same log — single source of truth, no nightly extract jobs.

sections.heading: Why Kafka, not just the SQL log
sections.body: Many independent downstream consumers (fraud detection, tax engine, user analytics, regulatory reporting, per-region replication) want to tail wallet events at their own pace. Kafka is a shared commit log; querying the SQL ledger every minute from each of them would crush it.

gained: Segmented storage model scales tail storage cheaply

bottlenecks.title: Exactly-once producer coupling stalls the transfer commit path
bottlenecks.trigger: The design calls for transactional producer semantics (Debezium outbox or KIP-939 XA) to couple Kafka publish with the MySQL XA COMMIT across shard_3 and shard_11. At 350 peak transfer TPS, a single broker leader election (10-30s), ISR shrink below min.insync.replicas=2, or partition unavailability blocks the producer's commitTransaction call — which sits on the critical path after XA COMMIT and before the API's 201 response
bottlenecks.symptom: Transfer latency spikes from ~80ms to seconds+, coordinator_log entries pile up in COMMITTING state with both shards already committed but Kafka publish hanging, API replicas exhaust concurrency=3000 waiting on coord, LB ejects API replicas on 5xx, users see 'transfer failed' for transactions that actually moved money — a correctness-looking incident that is really a publish-lag incident
bottlenecks.mitigation: Decouple publish from the hot path using a transactional outbox: coordinator writes the event row to a MySQL outbox table in the same COMMITTING transaction, and a Debezium CDC connector tails the binlog to Kafka asynchronously. Publish lag becomes a data-freshness problem (bounded by CDC), not a transfer-latency problem. Set producer max.block.ms=2000 as a safety cap; acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 stays, but is off the synchronous user path
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on producer p99 send latency > 500ms sustained 1min, transaction_abort_rate > 0.1%, outbox_unpublished_age > 30s (CDC lag), and any correlation between Kafka broker events and coordinator COMMITTING->COMMITTED transition time > 200ms

bottlenecks.title: Partition hotspotting on high-volume merchant/creator account keys
bottlenecks.trigger: Events on wallet.transfer.committed and wallet.balance.changed are keyed by account_id (or txn_id → account-derived) to preserve per-account ordering for downstream fraud/analytics consumers. With 500M accounts but skewed traffic (a viral creator or merchant receiving 10-100x normal TPS), a single partition can absorb 20-50 events/sec while siblings sit near zero. At 30M events/day (~350 event/sec peak) across e.g. 64 partitions, the expected 5-6 events/sec/partition becomes 60+ on hot partitions
bottlenecks.symptom: Per-partition consumer lag on wallet.transfer.committed grows only on specific partitions — fraud consumer falls 5-30 minutes behind for hot-account events while other partitions are caught up; fraud decisions on the hot account are stale (the exact account most likely to need fraud review); broker disk I/O imbalanced across nodes; adding consumer instances doesn't help because the bottleneck is single-partition throughput
bottlenecks.mitigation: For high-throughput accounts, switch keying to account_id + sub_bucket (4-16 buckets) so events fan across multiple partitions; consumers that need strict per-account ordering perform a final in-memory merge by account_id. Alternatively, publish hot-account events to a dedicated high-partition-count topic (wallet.transfer.committed.hot) routed via a producer-side classifier. Pre-identify merchant/platform accounts and pre-shard them
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on per-partition produce_rate > 3x cluster median sustained 5min, per-partition consumer_lag > 10000 messages while other partitions < 1000, and broker disk_io skew > 40% across nodes; weekly report of top-20 keys by event count

bottlenecks.title: Tiered storage and 7-year retention cost/recall explosion
bottlenecks.trigger: Retention policy is 7 days hot on Kafka + tiered to S3 for 7-year compliance retention. At 15 GB/day × 365 × 7 = 38 TB total, plus 3x replication on the hot tier (7 days × 15 GB × 3 = 315 GB hot) — manageable in steady state, but a compliance subpoena or regulatory audit requesting 'all transfers for user X from 2023' requires scanning months of tiered segments. Kafka's S3 tiered storage read path is not indexed by key, so range scans pull full segments
bottlenecks.symptom: Audit/compliance queries take hours-to-days instead of minutes; S3 egress bills spike on audit cycles; a regulator deadline (SOX/PCI) forces emergency re-ingestion of tiered data back to hot storage, saturating brokers and causing producer backpressure on the live path; cold-tier schema evolution breaks because consumers can't read old Avro/Protobuf versions
bottlenecks.mitigation: Don't treat Kafka as the primary audit query store — sink wallet.transfer.committed to an indexed cold store (S3 + Iceberg/Parquet partitioned by date+account_id, or a columnar warehouse like Snowflake/BigQuery) via a dedicated consumer. Keep Kafka tiered storage as the replay spine only. Enforce schema registry with backward-compatible evolution and include schema_id in every event. Pre-compute per-account monthly aggregates for common audit queries
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on S3 tiered-storage read_bytes > 10x baseline (signals audit scan), cold_tier_segment_age vs hot_tier cutover lag > 1 day (tiering falling behind), and schema_registry incompatible_evolution_count > 0; track audit-query p99 and alert if > 5 min

prebuild.explanation: ### Why Kafka is here for a digital wallet For a PayPal/Venmo-style wallet, a committed transfer isn't just interesting to the two users involved — it's interesting to the **fraud team** (is this a suspicious pattern?), the **compliance team** (SOX + PCI require 7-year audit trails on every money movement), the **analytics team** (daily active users, transfer volume), the **tax engine**, and possibly a **per-region replica** for regulatory data residency. Each of those consumers wants to read every transfer event, independently, at their own pace. Kafka is the shared commit log that lets all of them tail the same event stream without any of them knowing about each other, and without any of them querying the ledger directly. ### What happens without it Remove Kafka and every downstream consumer has to poll the MySQL ledger. Fraud wants events within seconds, so it runs `SELECT * FROM ledger_entries WHERE posted_at >?` every 5 seconds across all 16 shards. Analytics does the same on a different cadence. Compliance does a nightly extract. Now the ledger — which is already busy holding XA locks during 2PC transfers — is also serving dozens of range-scan queries from internal teams. Transfer p99 latency spikes, on-call sees lock contention, and users see \"transfer failed\" errors while a data engineer's job runs. ### The number **30M events/day ≈ 350 events/sec peak, ~15 GB/day, 38 TB over 7 years.** A single Kafka topic with a handful of partitions absorbs 350 events/sec trivially, and tiered storage to S3 after 7 days keeps hot-tier costs bounded while preserving the 7-year audit retention compliance demands. ### Trade-off The designer accepted the complexity of keeping Kafka publishes atomic with MySQL commits (via transactional outbox / CDC) in exchange for decoupling every downstream consumer from the ledger's hot path.

operations.title: P2P transfer A→B (ACID, 2PC)
operations.name: P2P transfer A→B (ACID, 2PC)
operations.description: Alice sends $100 to Bob. Accounts live on different MySQL shards, triggering the 2PC path. Either both balance updates commit or neither does.

steps.title: Alice taps Send on the mobile app
steps.action: Alice has confirmed the transfer details. The app POSTs with a UUIDv4 idempotency key that it will reuse on any retry.
steps.codeOrCommand:
POST /v1/transfers HTTP/1.1
Host: wallet.example.com
Authorization: Bearer <jwt>
Idempotency-Key: 8c3e9a1d-... { "from_account": "acct_alice", "to_account": "acct_bob", "amount_minor": 10000, "currency": "USD", "memo": "lunch"
}

steps.title: LB picks a Wallet API replica
steps.action: Least-connections routing. mTLS re-originated for the inward hop.
steps.codeOrCommand:
upstream = pool.pick(algo="least_connections", healthy_only=True)
forward(req → upstream, mtls=true)

steps.title: API validates request shape and delegates auth
steps.action: API checks amount_minor is a positive integer, currencies match, from_account ownership claim exists in the JWT. Then calls Auth for full token validation.
steps.codeOrCommand:
assert isinstance(body.amount_minor, int) and body.amount_minor > 0
assert body.currency in ISO_4217
assert jwt.claims.sub == owner_of(body.from_account) # claim-level check
auth_result = auth.verify(jwt, step_up_required=body.amount_minor >= STEP_UP_THRESHOLD)

steps.title: Auth validates JWT + device binding
steps.action: Verifies JWT signature/expiry, checks the revocation blacklist, confirms device binding. $100 is below the step-up threshold so no MFA challenge.
steps.codeOrCommand:
claims = jwt_verify(token, pubkey)
assert not revocation_cache.contains(claims.jti)
assert device_binding[claims.sub].contains(device_fingerprint)

steps.title: Coordinator allocates txn_id and writes PREPARING state
steps.action: The coordinator durably records its intent BEFORE touching either shard. This is the crash-recovery anchor — if the coordinator dies now, recovery knows to abort.
steps.note: Because acct_alice and acct_bob land on different shards, we're in the 2PC path. Same-shard transfers skip this coordination entirely and run as a single local transaction.

steps.title: PREPARE on shard_3 (debit Alice) — holds locks
steps.action: Shard 3 runs the debit under an XA-prepared transaction. Crucially, the `balance_minor >=:amt` predicate guards against overdraft — if insufficient funds, 0 rows are updated and PREPARE votes NO.
steps.codeOrCommand:
-- on shard_3 (Alice's home shard)
XA START 'tx_01HWXB...'; UPDATE account_balances
SET balance_minor = balance_minor - 10000, version = version + 1, updated_at = now(6)
